references.text: The immediately preceding verse: To all who received him, he gave the right to become children of God—to those who believe in his name. Verse 13 explains that this right as children does not originate from human sources but from God ([ref:Joh 1:12|John 1:12]).

Jesus explains to Nicodemus that one must be born again—born of the Spirit, not of flesh. This expands on the thought in John 1:13 that children of God are not born of human will but of God ([ref:Joh 3:3-8|John 3:3-8]).
James writes that God "by his own will gave us birth through the word of truth". This confirms that new birth is according to God’s will, not man’s ([ref:Jak 1:18|James 1:18]).
Peter praises God who "in his great mercy has given us new birth into a living hope". New birth is attributed to God’s mercy, not human will or blood ([ref:1 Pet 1:3|1 Peter 1:3]).

Peter says that believers are "born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God". This emphasizes that new birth does not come from anything human or perishable ([ref:1 Pet 1:23|1 Peter 1:23]).

John writes that whoever is born of God does not practice sin, because God’s seed remains in them. The expression "born of God" directly connects to John 1:13 and the divine origin of believers’ new life ([ref:1 Joh 3:9|1 John 3:9]).
"Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God." This confirms that new birth—being born of God—is linked to faith, not to human blood or will ([ref:1 Joh 5:1|1 John 5:1]).

"Everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world." The expression "born of God" (ἐκ θεοῦ γεγεννημένον) is the same as in John 1:13 and emphasizes the divine origin of believers ([ref:1 Joh 5:4|1 John 5:4]).

Paul distinguishes between children of the flesh and children of the promise. What matters is not natural descent but God’s promise—a thought that aligns with the idea that it is not blood or human will that makes someone a child of God ([ref:Rom 9:8|Romans 9:8]).

"So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who shows mercy." This emphasizes that salvation and adoption do not come from man’s will (θέλημα ἀνδρός) but from God’s sovereign action ([ref:Rom 9:16|Romans 9:16]).

Paul distinguishes between those born according to the flesh and those born according to the Spirit, using an allegory about Isaac and Ishmael. This addresses the same contrast as John 1:13 between human and divine origin ([ref:Gal 4:28-29|Galatians 4:28-29]).

Paul writes that God saved us "not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit". Salvation and new birth are God’s work, not human will ([ref:Tit 3:5|Titus 3:5]).

Paul writes that God, being rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. Salvation is entirely God’s initiative, not man’s will or effort ([ref:Ef 2:4-5|Ephesians 2:4-5]).
